text: In July 1497, four vessels gathered at Belém for a voyage into the ocean.
The men walked in procession to the shore, carrying candles, praying before departure.
At the water's edge, Vasco da Gama and his captains boarded the waiting boats.
They loosed the sails, caught the river wind, and stood down the Tagus.
Behind the flagships sailed a heavy store-ship, carrying provisions for three long years.
Passing the stone tower of Bugio, the ships met the rolling swells of the open sea.
Four hulls fell into line, keeping watch upon one another under full sail.
Night fell over the Atlantic as the fleet lantern was lit upon the flagship's stern.
By late July, the volcanic peak of Tenerife loomed through the morning mist.
At Santiago in Cape Verde, they took on water and meat before turning into the deep ocean.
Entering the doldrums, the sails went slack under a blistering equatorial sun.
Da Gama turned southwest into the open sea, making the great arc to catch the southern winds.
For ninety-six days they saw neither shore nor sail, surrounded only by phosphorescent waters.
Swells battered the oak hulls, forcing the crew to mend cordage and pump water day and night.
In late October, gannets and floating gulfweed signaled land was drawing near.
On the seventh of November, the armada dropped anchor in the shelter of St. Helena Bay.
A barter ashore turned violent; spears flew, and Da Gama was struck in the leg.
Beating south into fierce head-winds, the ships strained against freezing Antarctic gales.
Through tearing sea-fog, the jagged black cliffs of the Cape of Storms appeared.
On the twenty-second of November, with wind astern, the fleet rounded the southern tip of Africa.
At Mossel Bay, they broke up and burned the damaged store-ship, dividing its cargo.
The local pastoralists played reed flutes and traded an ox for red caps and brass bells.
On a rocky height above the bay, they raised a stone cross and the royal arms of Portugal.
Sailing onward, the ferocious Agulhas current pushed against the bows with immense power.
At Inhambane, copper-wearing chieftains welcomed the mariners with gifts of fowl and millet.
Entering Quelimane, Da Gama named it the River of Good Omens after sighting Asian silk cloth.
A terrible sickness struck: mariners' gums swelled over their teeth and legs grew black with scurvy.
In March, the fleet anchored off Mozambique Island, entering the stone-built Swahili maritime world.
The Sultan of Mozambique came out in velvet robes, believing the newcomers to be Turkish merchants.
When the Sultan discovered they were Christians, hostility broke out and Da Gama fired his bombards.
Local pilots hired to guide the armada attempted to run the ships onto shallow coastal reefs.
The fleet slipped away under cover of darkness, sailing north into perilous uncharted waters.
At Mombasa, night swimmers slipped through the harbor attempting to cut the flagship's anchor cables.
Suspecting betrayal, Da Gama dropped boiling oil on two captured captives to extract the plot.
Cutting their lines at dawn, the Portuguese fled Mombasa before the harbor boats could surround them.
On Easter Sunday, they reached the whitewashed walls and coconut groves of friendly Malindi.
The King of Malindi rowed out in a crimson damask barge, greeting the captain-major as an ally.
Gujarati merchants came aboard the flagship, celebrating the arrival with bronze horns and revelry.
Here, the King granted them a master pilot who knew every reef and wind of the Indian Ocean.
On the twenty-fourth of April, the fleet cast off from Africa into the boundless Arabian Sea.
The southwest monsoon caught the square sails, driving the three caravels eastward at fierce speed.
Each evening on the quarterdeck, the pilot lifted his wooden kamal to measure the height of the North Star.
For three unbroken weeks, sapphire rolling swells stretched from horizon to horizon.
Schools of flying fish skimmed across the crests, and banded sea serpents drifted past the hull.
A mid-ocean gale tested the strained timbers, but the seasoned hulls held fast against the tempest.
On the eighteenth of May, floating palm fronds and coastal birds signaled India was at hand.
Through the ocean haze, the majestic blue summit of Mount Delli rose above the waters.
The pilot pointed toward the lush coast: 'This is the land you sought — this is Calicut.'
On the twentieth of May 1498, the Portuguese armada anchored off the palm shores of Kappad.
Sent ashore, a convict was greeted by North Africans in Spanish: 'What devil brought you here?'
Carried in shaded palanquins through packed streets, Da Gama marched into Calicut amid roaring crowds.
Entering a Hindu temple filled with brass sculptures, the mariners mistakenly prayed to what they thought was Mary.
The Zamorin reclined upon a green velvet couch in his palace, spitting betel nut into a golden basin.
When the Portuguese presented their gifts of wash-basins, hats, and sugar, royal ministers laughed in scorn.
In a tense second audience, Da Gama defended his King, demanding trade in spices, rubies, and gold.
Arab merchants warned the Zamorin that these strangers were corsairs, turning the court against them.
Detained ashore in Pandarani, Da Gama wrote to the ships to send ransom goods to secure his release.
Trade factor Diogo Dias managed to purchase modest samples of cloves, cinnamon, and pepper.
Suspicions erupted; guards seized Dias's warehouse, while a loyal servant swam out to alert the fleet.
Da Gama struck back, seizing eighteen Malabar merchants aboard the flagship as hostages for his men.
An exchange was brokered: Dias returned bearing the Zamorin's palm-leaf letter to King Manuel.
Seventy armed war boats swarmed the becalmed fleet until a sudden thunderstorm carried the Portuguese to sea.
At the Anjediva Islands, the battered ships careened their weed-fouled hulls and filled fresh water casks.
A mysterious merchant landed, speaking fluent Venetian. It was Gaspar da Gama — the voyage's greatest prize.
